title: Photo tour: Western Sydney International Airport & The Rayleigh Lounge
body:
Sydney has a new gateway to the world. Western Sydney International (or Nancy-Bird Walton Airport) is now open at Badgerys Creek, around 50 kilometres west of the CBD. Designed to take pressure off Sydney Airport while bringing travel closer to the city’s growing western suburbs, it’s a major new chapter for Australia’s biggest city.
Unlike Kingsford Smith, the new airport operates around the clock, without a curfew. That gives airlines greater flexibility to schedule overnight flights and opens up more opportunities for international connections.
The airport welcomed its first passenger flights on 25 October 2026, with Jetstar operating the inaugural service to the Gold Coast. International services include Air New Zealand flights to Auckland and Singapore Airlines’ upcoming daily connection to Singapore. Join us on a photo tour around the terminal and the international Rayleigh Lounge.
Inside the WSI terminal
The terminal has a contemporary, open design, with plenty of natural light and a clean, modern aesthetic. Its layout has been designed to support both domestic and international operations, with passenger facilities that can grow as traffic increases.
You’ll find departures on the left, where the check-in hall predominantly consists of self-serve kiosks. There’s also a premium check-in booth nearby that we understand will be used by select full-service airlines.
Upstairs, you’ll find security screening and the main departures hall. International passengers need to scan their boarding passes at a gate on the left, while domestic passengers can proceed straight to security on the right.
There are practical touches throughout the terminal, including free Wi-Fi, charging points, drinking water stations and flight information displays.
Over at the gates, the waiting areas are bright and airy with great views of the airfield. Gates 19A/B, 20A/B and 21A/B all serve domestic flights. Each A/B pair can operate individually for smaller aircraft, or in tandem to service larger widebodies simultaneously.
Gates 22A/B to 25 A/B will service international flights, but all of those except for 25A/B are also ‘swing gates’. These are capable of serving either domestic or international flights, depending on the way the partitions are set up.
First look at the Rayleigh Lounge
For eligible international passengers, the Rayleigh Lounge adds a premium space to the new airport experience. Operated by dnata, the lounge is located on the terminal’s mezzanine level, with expansive views across the airfield towards the Blue Mountains. Look right as you exit immigration to find the lift or escalator up to the lounge.
The Rayleigh Lounge has been designed to accommodate different types of travellers, with dedicated dining and lounge areas, a feature bar and an open kitchen. Whether you’re looking for somewhere to work before a flight or simply want to settle in with a drink, there are several spaces to choose from.
While there wasn’t any food on display at this preview, the drinks list ranges from Oyster Bay Sauvignon Blanc to Carlton Draught and Corona Extra. Spirits are also available.
Lounge seating and design
Inside, the lounge combines contemporary styling with a distinctly Australian feel. Timber finishes and softer textures help create a welcoming atmosphere, while different seating arrangements give solo travellers, couples and groups options for spending their time.
There is also a dedicated dining area and a feature bar, helping separate the more social parts of the lounge from quieter spaces to relax. The Rayleigh Lounge initially has capacity for around 80 guests, although it has been designed to expand to approximately 130 as passenger demand grows.
WSI passenger facilities and amenities
Beyond the main departure and arrival areas, WSI includes a range of facilities designed to make the airport more accessible and comfortable. These include accessible family rooms, sensory spaces, multi-faith prayer and quiet rooms, hearing loop technology and pet relief areas.
There’s not much open in the main terminal at the moment. There’s a well-stocked Relay store selling snacks, medicines, entertainment, travel gear and more. You’ll also find a small café in the food court and a tech store near the gates. Craving bubble tea? A Gong Cha is also slated to open soon.
There’s signage and space set aside for a domestic premium lounge, but we haven’t heard any details on that yet. Past this future domestic lounge area is the exit back down to the arrivals hall. The baggage belts are pretty long, so there’s plenty of space for everyone. You’ll also find car hire counters on your left when you exit.
The public bus is currently the most cost-effective way to travel to and from WSI, at least until the Metro opens. The free WSI Link bus departs every 30 minutes to St Marys railway station. From there, you can then catch a regular train to the city. The journey takes about 95 minutes to Central if you have a good connection, and costs under $6.
There’s also the SuperShuttle WSI, which costs $25 per person to Parramatta, $55 to Sydney CBD or $65 to Sydney Airport. You can also order taxis and rideshares near the front, including a dedicated Uber pickup zone.
The bus stops are located to the right of the airport when you’re exiting (or the left if you’re heading in). It’s a few minutes’ walk from the departures side of the terminal.
Summing up
Western Sydney International is a significant addition to Australia’s aviation landscape. Its 24-hour operating model, modern terminal and growing list of airline partners give travellers across Western Sydney another option for getting around Australia and overseas.
The Rayleigh Lounge is a welcome part of that proposition, offering eligible international passengers a comfortable place to relax, dine or freshen up before departure.
While both the airport and lounge will evolve as passenger numbers grow, this first look offers an encouraging glimpse of what Western Sydney’s new aviation gateway has to offer.
Disclaimer: Terminal photos by Brandon Loo, who travelled at Point Hacks’ expense. Rayleigh Lounge photos by Joshua Weckert, who travelled at Point Hacks’ expense.
